Overview

Cairo as a Business Centre

Cairo is the largest city in Egypt and the centre of its commercial, financial and administrative life. Cairo Governorate had an estimated population of about 10.2 million in January 2023, and Greater Cairo extends well beyond that across Giza and Qalyubia. The Egyptian Exchange, the Central Bank of Egypt and the head offices of most major banks, contractors, real estate developers and holding companies are in the metropolitan area. Government has been moving to the New Administrative Capital, which became the official seat of national government in April 2024, while planned satellite cities such as New Cairo host corporate headquarters, industrial zones and large residential and retail projects.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Cairo because most significant Egyptian counterparties, whether listed companies, family-owned groups, developers or state-linked enterprises, are run from the city. Foreign investors, lenders and suppliers need to understand who controls a Cairo company, how it is connected to other businesses and to public bodies, and what disputes it has faced. Shareholder and beneficial ownership information filed with authorities is not publicly accessible, so research relies on gazettes, listed-company disclosures, court and press records and careful source work. Cairo is also a regional seat for arbitration, and parties to CRCICA proceedings often need background and asset research.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Cairo

01

Family group and holding company mapping

Mapping the companies, directors and relationships around Cairo-based family groups and holding companies, using GAFI Investment Gazette notices, commercial register inquiries, EGX disclosures and press archives, where shareholder lists filed with GAFI are not publicly disclosed and control often sits with relatives or nominees.

02

Real estate developer due diligence

Reviewing developers and contractors active in New Cairo, the New Administrative Capital and other new cities for investors and lenders, including project histories, delivery disputes, litigation, links to land allocators and the financial pressures behind large off-plan sales programmes.

03

State-linked counterparty screening

Identifying whether a Cairo counterparty has links to public bodies, state-owned enterprises or politically exposed persons, which matters for anti-corruption compliance and for understanding how a contract or licence was obtained in a market where the state is a major economic actor.

04

Asset research for CRCICA and court matters

Supporting counsel in Cairo-seated arbitrations and Egyptian court proceedings with background on parties and identification of assets, including listed shareholdings, known real estate and corporate interests, while recognising that land registration is incomplete and many records are reachable only through Egyptian lawyers.

05

Distributor and agent integrity reviews

Assessing Cairo-based commercial agents, distributors and importers before appointment or after a compliance concern, covering ownership, reputation, government relationships, prior disputes and red flags around commissions, customs and procurement in consumer goods, healthcare and industrial supply.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Cairo

Courts sitting in Cairo

Egypt's Court of Cassation and Supreme Constitutional Court sit in Cairo, as do the Cairo Court of Appeal and Cairo's courts of first instance. Specialised economic courts hear many commercial, banking, capital markets and investment disputes, and EGX's chairman has described them, together with arbitration and specialised settlement bodies, as part of the dispute system for the financial sector. Judgments are only partly published, so litigation research usually needs Egyptian counsel.

CRCICA and specialised dispute bodies

The Cairo Regional Centre for International Commercial Arbitration (CRCICA) is the main arbitral institution in the city and administers domestic and international cases. For the non-banking financial sector, the Egyptian Center for Arbitration and Settlement of Non-Banking Financial Disputes (ECAS) also operates. Arbitration parties frequently need research on opposing parties, their corporate structures and assets to assess claims and enforcement.

Commercial register and GAFI

Companies are incorporated through GAFI's Investor Service Center and then entered in the Commercial Register, administered by the Internal Trade Development Authority under the Ministry of Supply and Internal Trade. Basic existence and status checks are available online, and GAFI's Investment Gazette publishes incorporation decisions and articles. Beneficial ownership records are restricted to authorised officials, and shareholder lists and private company accounts are not published.

New cities and land authorities

Satellite cities in Cairo Governorate, including New Cairo and the New Administrative Capital, are planned and governed by the New Urban Communities Authority, which handles land sales and zoning, while the governorate handles policing and some services. Property and developer research therefore involves NUCA allocations and developer records as well as ordinary registration, which is known to be incomplete in Egypt.

Financial sector institutions

The Central Bank of Egypt, the Egyptian Exchange and the Financial Regulatory Authority, which supervises non-banking financial activity including capital markets and listed issuers, are central to Cairo's financial system. Listed companies publish disclosures through EGX, which makes the listed sector considerably more transparent than private groups. Regulatory sanctions and disclosures are useful sources in counterparty reviews of Cairo groups with listed affiliates.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Cairo

TDSC handles Cairo matters from Nashville and has no office, staff or licence in Egypt. Engagements start by setting what can lawfully be established from outside the country: GAFI and EGX publications, commercial register status checks, regulatory notices, court information available through counsel, press archives in Arabic and English, and international records. Because the position of private investigation in Egypt is unclear and some inquiries raise security sensitivities, TDSC does not commission surveillance or approaches to officials, and any local enquiries are scoped with Egyptian counsel. Personal data is handled with Egypt's data protection law in mind, and reports separate confirmed facts from reported information.

TDSC has no office in Cairo. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Cairo: Frequently Asked Questions

Can we find out who owns a private company in Cairo?

Partly. Commercial register inquiries confirm that a company exists and its status, and GAFI's Investment Gazette publishes incorporation decisions and articles. Shareholder lists filed with GAFI are not publicly disclosed, and beneficial ownership records are open only to authorised officials. Ownership is therefore reconstructed from gazette notices, disclosures, litigation and press, and conclusions are stated with their limits.

Is CRCICA a common choice for disputes involving Cairo companies?

Yes. The Cairo Regional Centre for International Commercial Arbitration is the best known arbitral institution in Egypt and handles domestic and international cases. Choice of institution and seat is a matter for counsel. TDSC supports parties in CRCICA and other proceedings with research on counterparties, witnesses and assets.

Do new cities such as New Cairo raise particular diligence issues?

They can. Land in the new cities is allocated and governed by the New Urban Communities Authority, and large off-plan projects depend on developers' financing and delivery track records. Diligence on developers and land holdings looks at allocation history, project delays, disputes with buyers and contractors, and links between developers and other groups.

Can TDSC carry out surveillance in Cairo?

No. We have not identified a licensing regime that authorises private investigators in Egypt, and surveillance, photography of certain sites and approaches to officials can raise security concerns. TDSC's Cairo work is documentary and open-source research, with any local enquiries scoped with Egyptian counsel so that they remain lawful.

How useful are Egyptian court records in background research?

They are useful but hard to reach. Judgments are only partly published and there is no comprehensive open search of Cairo court files. Litigation history is usually established through Egyptian counsel, published decisions, regulatory notices and press reporting, and the results are presented with a clear statement of coverage.
